Copper-Catalyzed Asymmetric Cyanation of Propargylic Radicals
Derived From Silyl-Substituted Allenes and Alkynes
Zhongming Cheng+, Guoyu Zhang+, Yunshun Deng, Yiping Zhang, Xiang Li, Pinhong Chen,
and Guosheng Liu*
Abstract: Here, we report an efficient method to
synthesize enantiomerically enriched propargyl nitriles
via copper-catalyzed asymmetric cyanation of propar-
gylic radicals, which are generated from silyl-substituted
allenes or alkynes. These reactions proceeded through a
highly site-selective hydrogen atom abstraction (HAA)
with Cu(II)-bound nitrogen-centered radicals (NCRs).
Notably, silyl-substituted allenes demonstrate excep-
tional allenic sp<sup>2</sup> C─H bond activation selectivity, out-
competing alternative reactive sp<sup>3</sup> C─H bonds (benzylic,
allylic, and heteroatom-adjacent) in HAA processes. This
chemo-selectivity profile enables precise enantiocontrol
and site-specific functionalization of complex molecular
architectures.
Introduction
Optically pure alkynyl moieties are extensively found in
natural products, pharmaceuticals, and material science.<sup>[1–4]</sup>
Moreover, enantioenriched alkynes also serve as valuable
building blocks for the synthesis of chiral compounds
and biologically active molecules.<sup>[5–7]</sup> Therefore, the syn-
thesis of chiral alkynes has garnered significant attention
over the past decades,<sup>[8–10]</sup> and the approaches to chi-
ral propargylic compounds include nucleophilic addition
of carbonyls,<sup>[11,12]</sup> hydroalkynylation,<sup>[13,14]</sup> and so on. In
recent years, substantial advancements have been achieved
via transition metal-catalyzed asymmetric radical cou-
pling reactions.<sup>[15–21]</sup> For instance, the pioneering stud-
ies on Ni-catalyzed asymmetric cross-coupling of propar-
gylic halides to organozinc reagents have been reported
by Fu and coworkers.<sup>[22,23]</sup> Very recently, the groups of
Liu<sup>[24–26]</sup> and Zhang<sup>[27,28]</sup> reported copper-catalyzed asym-
metric Sonogashira-type cross-couplings, which are compati-
ble with a broad range of terminal alkynes and prochiral alkyl
halides, respectively. However, as an alternative approach,
the asymmetric propargylic C─H functionalization reaction is
extremely rare.<sup>[29,30]</sup>
Asymmetric catalytic C─H functionalization presents a
more attractive and streamlined approach for the synthesis
of functional molecules.<sup>[31–34]</sup> With a copper-catalyzed radical
relay process,<sup>[35]</sup> enantioselective functionalization reactions
of benzylic <sup>[36,37]</sup> and allylic C─H bonds <sup>[38]</sup> have been
recently developed. Inspired by these studies, we reasoned
that enantiomerically enriched propargylic compounds could
be obtained through this radical relay process. Distinct
from previous studies, however, propargylic radicals as key
intermediates involved in the reaction can be tautomerized
to allenic radicals, thus leading to the formation of the
corresponding alkyne and/or allene products, respectively
(Scheme 1a).<sup>[39–43]</sup> For instance, we recently reported the
enantioselective cyanation of propargylic C─H bonds of aryl-
substituted alkynes <sup>[44]</sup> and the enantioselective cyanation
of allenic C─H bonds of allenes,<sup>[45,46]</sup> where both reactions
involve the same tautomers of propargylic and allenic radicals,
and the radical coupling of Cu(II) cyanide exclusively occurs
at less steric allenic radicals, providing the cyano-allene
products exclusively (Scheme 1b). Can we explore novel
C─H functionalization strategies by modulating site- and
chemo-selectivity to enable the efficient synthesis of chiral
propargylic nitrile products? Herein, we communicate the
first copper-catalyzed asymmetric cyanation of propargylic
radicals generated from silyl-substituted allenes or alkynes,
which serve as the limiting C─H reagents (Scheme 1c). The
hydrogen atom abstraction (HAA) process demonstrated
remarkable site-selectivity, occurring exclusively at sp<sup>2</sup> allenic
C─H bonds adjacent to silyl groups. Furthermore, distinct
from previous studies, the radical coupling of Cu(II) cyanide
exhibited chemoselective preference, proceeding through the
less sterically hindered propargylic radical pathway.
Results and Discussion

catalyzed cyanation, arylation, and alkynylation reactions of

Results and Discussion

allenic C─H bonds, where a highly site-selective HAA with
Cu(II)-bound nitrogen-centered radicals (NCRs) is critical to
the success of the C─H bond functionalizations of allenes;
however, mono-alkyl-substituted allenes were proven to be
ineffective candidates for these reactions. Considering the
nature of easily deprotected silyl groups, silyl-substituted
allene 1, acting as the “masked” terminal allenes, was chosen
to carry out the asymmetric C─H cyanation. As mentioned
in Scheme 2a, based on the previous studies, the HAA
could occur at the C1 (H<sup>a</sup>) and C3 (H<sup>b</sup>) positions, which
generate two kinds of allenic radicals. I and III, and their
resonances II and IV. The final radical coupling process by
sterically bulky chiral L*Cu(II) cyanide is more favorable to
trap the less sterically hindered carbon-centered radicals;<sup>[49]</sup>
Therefore, the reaction is likely to yield the corresponding
alkynyl nitriles 2 and/or allenyl nitriles 2-, which can be readily
converted to the terminal alkynyl and allenyl nitriles. These
compounds have been recognized as important synthons in
organic synthesis.
Encouraged by the above hypothesis, we commenced
our initial study on the reaction of allene 1a and TMSCN
with NF-1 as an NCR precursor. We were delighted that
the reaction afforded the desired alkynyl nitrile product
2a exclusively, while the previously reported allene nitrile
product
\mathbf { 2 } \mathbf { a } ^ { \prime }
was not observed (Scheme 2b). After careful
screening, the propargyl cyanide product 2a was obtained
in 98% yield with specific site-selectivity
( \mathbf { C } _ { s p 2 } { : } \mathbf { C } _ { s p 3 } > 2 0 { : } 1 )
and good enantioselectivity (81% ee) in the presence of
0.5 mol%
\mathrm { C u ( C H _ { 3 } C N ) _ { 4 } P F _ { 6 } / \mathbf { L 1 } }
(Scheme 2b-i, entry 1).
Notably, some features were observed in this reaction. First,
different NCR precursors exhibited significant influences
on both yields and ee values. For instance, NF-2 exhibited
relatively lower reactivity but similar enantioselectivity
(entry 2), while NF-3 displayed moderate reactivity but
with poor yields and diminished enantioselectivity (entry
3). In contrast,
^ { t } \mathbf { B u O } _ { 2 } \mathbf { B } \mathbf { z }
was demonstrated as an ineffective
radical precursor toward the C─H cyanation (entry 4).
Second, various solvents could provide excellent yields
but slightly affect the enantioselectivity (entries 5–8). For
example, a 71% ee was obtained in acetonitrile, while similar
results were given in acetone and perfluorobenzene. Third,
ligand screening revealed that, as shown in Scheme 2b-ii,
increasing the steric bulk of groups at the gem-carbon
position was proven to be ineffective, which could decrease
the enantioselectivity (e.g., 72% ee for L2). Considering the
linear and rod-like structure of triple bonds in propargylic
radicals, the designed L3, by extending the chiral pocket,
could slightly improve the enantioselectivity to 83% ee, albeit
with a reduced reactivity (68% yield). Further prolonging
the reaction time could give the desired product an excellent
yield (96%, Scheme 2b-iii). Finally, modifying the silyl groups
could also affect the enantioselectivity. Although the trialkyl
silyl-substituted substrates gave similar results (e.g., 2b, 2c),
introducing the phenyl group into silyl groups could improve
the enantioselectivity up to 90% ee (e.g., 2d, 2e).
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, a variety
of silyl-substituted allenes with dimethylphenylsilyl groups
were investigated (Scheme 2c). For the substrates with simple
alkyl chains, the reactions consistently furnished the desired
propargyl nitriles (2f–2l) in nearly quantitative isolated yields
(92%–98%) and excellent enantioselectivities (88%–95%
ee). Moreover, substrates bearing various functional groups
compatible with the reaction conditions, such as halide (2m),
CF (2n), silyl ether (2o), OTs (2p), imide (2q), and esters (2r,
2s), yielded the corresponding products in excellent results.
Substrates containing small rings (e.g., cyclopropyl
azeti-
dine 2s) were suitable for the reactions, and these high-strain
rings were retained. Moreover, heterocycles (e.g., pyridine
2t, oxazole 2u), and complex moieties (e.g., uridine 2v, gly-
cyrrhetinic ester 2w) were also compatible with the reaction
conditions, and the corresponding products were obtained in
excellent yields and ee (or de) values. All these outcomes
(typically > 90% yields) demonstrated the extremely high
catalytic reactivity toward allenic sp<sup>2</sup> C─H cyanation.

the asymmetric cyanation of propargylic C─H bonds, which
presents an alternative pathway for the synthesis of these
chiral propargylic nitriles. As shown in Scheme 3a, when the
silyl-substituted alkyne 3a was treated under the standard
conditions, the reaction indeed occurred and afforded the

Increasing the dosages of NF-1 and TMSCN (4.0 equiva-
lents) and prolonging the reaction time (72 h) could increase
a yield of 2f to 62% (90% ee). Notably, the identical product
2f was obtained with the same enantiomeric control as the
reaction of allenes, indicating that the reaction involved the
same tautomerization of two radical intermediates. Further
optimizing Box ligands (e.g., L4 and L5) by enhancing the
steric hindrance of the gem-groups failed to improve the
enantioselectivity.
Subsequently, the scope of alkyne substrates was also
examined (Scheme 3b). Similar to the allene substrates, a
range of silyl-alkynes featuring simple alkyl or functionalized
alkyl groups proved to be compatible with the reaction, deliv-
ering the corresponding products 4a–4e in moderate yields
(62%–72%) while maintaining excellent enantioselectivity
(87%–90% ee). Notably, verifying silyl substituents in alkynes
could slightly affect the enantioselectivity, where a substrate
with a small trimethylsilyl group provided a slightly lower
enantiomeric ratio (84% ee, 4f),<sup>[50]</sup> while a substrate with a
larger diphenylmethylsilyl group gave a higher ee value (93%
ee, 4g), which offers guidance for substrate design to reach
high ee value. More importantly, besides the silyl-substituted
alkynes, various tertiary carbon-substituted alkynes were also
suitable for the reaction to provide propargylic nitriles 4j,
4k in moderate yields (60%–62%) with excellent ee values
(90%–91%). The similar alkynes 4l, 4m containing ester
groups are also suitable for the reaction but with slightly
reduced enantioselectivities (81%–83% ee).
As mentioned above, significantly different performance
was observed between silyl-substituted allenes and alkynes,
though both reactions provide an identical product. To gain
more insights, a series of control experiments were conducted.
First, the kinetic isotopic effect was probed through parallel
experiments using 1b and d -1b (Scheme 4a). The KIE
value
( k _ { \mathrm { H } } / k _ { \mathrm { D } } = 2 . 0 )
revealed that the HAA of allenic sp<sup>2</sup>
C─H bonds contributes to the rate-determining step. In
comparison, a higher KIE value
( k _ { \mathrm { H } } / k _ { \mathrm { D } } = 5 . 0 )
was obtained
in the case of alkyne (3a and d -3a). In addition, the time
course of two reactions in Scheme 4b revealed that the
HAA of allenic
\mathrm { s p } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { C - H }
in 1b (one hydrogen) is 120
times faster than that of
\mathrm { s p } ^ { 3 } \ \mathrm { C - H }
in 3a (two hydrogens),
greatly affected by the bond dissociation energy (BDE) of
the allenic sp<sup>2</sup> C─H bond (82 kcal mol−<sup>1</sup>) which is lower
than that of propargylic sp<sup>3</sup> C─H bonds (86 kcal mol−<sup>1</sup>).<sup>[51]</sup>
This observation is also reflected by the remarkably different
KIE values. Second, this remarkable difference prompted
us to survey the site-selective HAA between various active
C─H bonds in allene and alkyne substrates. As shown in
Scheme 4c the reaction of allene 1c occurred at the allenic
sp<sup>2</sup> C─H<sup>1</sup> bond to deliver product 2d exclusively for 15 h,
while another active benzylic
\mathbf { s p } ^ { 3 } \mathbf { \Lambda } \mathbf { C } \mathbf { - } \mathbf { H }
bond was intact.
However, the reaction of alkyne 3b exhibited extremely poor
reactivity (16% yield) for 40 h, along with poor site-selectivity
( \mathrm { C } \mathrm { - } \mathrm { H } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { v s . } \ \mathrm { C } \mathrm { - } \mathrm { H } ^ { 3 } = 1 . 3 { : } 1 )
. These outcomes revealed that the
excellent site-selective HAA is much more likely to occur
at the allenic sp<sup>2</sup> C─H bond position of allenes rather than
that in alkynes. Therefore, various silyl-allenes containing
diverse active
\mathrm { s p } ^ { 3 } \mathrm { C - H }

examined (Scheme 3b). Similar to the allene substrates, a

groups are also suitable for the reaction but with slightly
reduced enantioselectivities (81%–83% ee).

(Scheme 5). First, the preparative utility of our method in
the laboratory was demonstrated by gram-scale reactions
(2d) with excellent yields and ee values. Chiral alkyl nitrile

cyanation of the benzylic C─H bond proceeded smoothly to
deliver a dinitrile product 8 in 90% yield with 97% de. Third,
hydrogenation of product 4d was conducted by Raney Ni
catalysts, which could provide the desired chiral alkyl amine
9 with almost identical ee values. After Pd/C hydrogenation,
it can be further oxidized to deliver alcohol product 10 in
60% yield with 87% ee. In addition, the reaction of 3c could
be scaled up to 6 mmol and yielded product 4f in 65% yield
(1.32 g) in 84% ee, which could be readily converted to
chiral terminal alkyne 11 in 81% yield without the erosion of
enantioselectivity.

Conclusion
In summary, we have developed a copper-catalyzed asymmet-
ric C─H cyanation of silyl-substituted allenes and alkynes,
providing easy access to chiral propargyl nitriles with excel-
lent enantioselectivity. The C─H functionalization reaction
occurred selectively at the allenic
\mathbf { s p } ^ { 2 } \mathbf { \Lambda } \mathbf { C } \mathbf { - } \mathbf { H }
bond position
of silyl-substituted allenes, or the propargylic
\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }
C─H bond
position of alkynes. Although both allenes and alkynes
yielded the same chiral propargylic nitriles, the reaction of
silyl-substituted allenes is significantly faster than that of the
corresponding alkynes, suggesting that HAA at the allenic
C─H bond position is more favorable than that at the
propargylic C─H bond position of alkynes. Moreover, the
reaction with allenes demonstrates exceptional selectivity for
the allenic C─H bond over various reactive
\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }
C─H bonds,
providing a promising platform for achieving highly selective
C─H bond functionalizations of complex molecules. Not only
does our presented methodology broaden the reaction types
of allenes and alkynes but also significantly enhances the
structural diversity of accessible products.
